snippets.text: - Good evening everyone.
I will call to order our regular meeting

of the Board of Directors
on this March 10th, 2026.

On behalf of the board,
welcome, and thank you
to those attending our meeting in person,
joining us by Zoom,
and those staying informed
by watching our recording at a later time.
The public is reminded

that if they wish to speak
during Community Comment,
they will need to fill out a speaker form

located in the back of the
room on the table to my left
and turn it in to our board secretary

seated at the end of our
table also on my left.
Comments will take place

during a designated Community
Comment portion of our agenda.
And before we get into tonight's agenda,
I want to take a moment

to introduce those seated
at the table with me.
To my right we have Superintendent Degner,
directors Horn-Frasier, Eastham, Williams.
To my left we have directors Finch, Lingo,

Vice President Abraham
is joining us via phone,
and Board Secretary Colvin.
And our first action for tonight
is approval of tonight's agenda.
Is there a motion?
- Move to approve the agenda for tonight.
- Second.

- Thank you. Board
secretary, ready to vote.
- Online voting is open.

All votes have been cast
and the motion carries
with all directors voting in favor.
- Thank you.

That takes us to our student
representative updates.

First up, we will have
Tate's video update.

- Sanaya.
- Jenna.

- [Jade] And Jade from Tate's
Media Productions team.

We were so glad to wrap
up the second trimester

and begin the last 12
weeks of the school year.
- [Sanaya] Our Tate Boys Basketball team
had a basketball scrimmage.
- [Jenna] Trimester 2 has come to the end.
Many students had received a couple awards
during the award ceremony.

- [Jade] We welcomed about
20 new transfer students
for the third trimester.
- [Sanaya] Spring break is soon to arrive.
We are excited for a break.

- [Jenna] A large group
of students had put a hand
to volunteer at various places
like the Shelter House books sale,

Houses and Homes, Skate City,
and the free lunch program.
- [Jade] We are hoping
the rest of the school year goes quickly.
- [Sanaya, Jade & Jenna] Toodles.

- All right, next up we
will have Liberty High.

John, I understand Mia's
unable to join us tonight.
- Yep. It's too bad.
So lots of stuff is going on.
In the past week we've had our finals
and those are finally over.

So we're in for the final
trimester, Trimester 3.

We hopefully don't have
too much more work.

I mean we have lots of
exams but they will go fast.
The next thing is athletics.
We had Boys Wrestling go to state.
Additionally, Natalie Ramsey,
one of our Liberty seniors, was named

the Mississippi Valley
Conference Athlete of the Year,
which we're very proud of.
Liberty's football coach was recognized
as the Coach of The year
for the 5A high school football teams
and then inspired by Waleed and Eddie
who are sadly not here right now,
we have a little outreach section.

So Ms. McGrain, an awesome
science teacher at Liberty,

took her engineering and
design class to the community
for inspiration for toy design.

So these engineering
students will look at toys,

see how they can improve
them or make them better

and then give those back to
children in the community.
Extracurriculars have been very busy.
The Science Bowl Team, including myself,
got to go to the State competition.
That was incredibly fun.
Liberty's Math Club

is preparing for the state
competition in Ames soon.

Science Olympiad also went
to the State competition,
taking home four medals

and going to the State
competition as well.
Performing arts, Jazz Band is tonight.

You guys should all definitely
come to our jazz concert
showing off all of Liberty's jazz bands.
And then Liberty Show Choir hosted events
with lots of other schools coming.
I'm not entirely aware of what they did,
but it was very cool.

And then finally,
Cheerleading and Color Guard
are hosting tryouts and clinics
for joining Color Guard next year.
That's all. Thank you.
- Great, thank you.
Next up we will have City High, Tobia,
I don't see Alma, so welcome.

- Yeah, a lot of solo
representation today.

As you can see, I brought
two gentlemen with me.
I'll introduce them in a moment,

but I'm gonna keep the recap
a little bit more brief.
So City High's Jazz Ensemble
won the Liberty Jazz Competition.
(attendees laugh)
And our Show Choir team, 4th Ave.,

won their third grand
championship this year

being the second high school
in Iowa in the history of Iowa
to have done so.

City High's art program
had our art show recently.
All of our very talented artists
got to show off what they made.

My friend made a lamp,
it was really heavy.

I had to help her carry it to
her from her car. So pity me.
Our Mock Trial team hosted a scrimmage,
Student Senate hosted our Winter Carnival,

which we've put on for
the past four years.
It was a lot of fun.
Our Quiz Ball team won a competition,
defended their title as state champions.

City High, another thing we
hosted was our math competition.
We qualified a few mathletes to State.
And finally I have these gentlemen.
Now if you all remember last week,
Alma and I brought along a representative
from our Show Choir team

to tell you a little bit
more about what they do.
These two are representatives

of our Business Professionals
of America clubs.
So they're gonna describe what they do
and then I'll finish up.
Get up here, guys.
- All right. How are you guys doing?
I'm doing great.

My name is, (laughs)
my name is Rami Vikali.
I'm the acting president
of our Business Professional of America.

I'm not here with my vice
president Rito Perez.
He couldn't be with us today.

But I'm with Joseph Hayek
who will be joining us.

And I just wanna talk a
little bit about our club.

So pretty much it was
just me and Rito left

after last year along with
a few sophomores and juniors

and we wanted to kind
of bring the club back.
We haven't gone to, yeah,

we haven't done a lot with
our club in quite some time.
So I thought it was the year to do that.
So we recruited over 20 members
and sort of just got the ground running
and we wanted to make a trip to State
and kind of make an impact there.

I'll have Joseph talk
about a little bit more
about what we did there.

- Yeah, so at State we had
two national qualifiers
and we ended up having one State champion,

which hadn't been done
at City High in 13 years.
So that was pretty incredible.
And then I think the main thing
I wanted to talk about up here
was how the reason that the City High BPA
is so important to City High
and we think it's important to City High
as it offers an experience

to such a wide variety
of different students,
because unlike other clubs,

it offers 50+ different events
in the sort of BPA world.

So we think it can cater to
lots of students' interests

and we think it's very
important to our school.

- Yeah, our whole goal is
just to bring the club back.
It was great to have a like make a trip
to State the first time in three years

and having that qualify
the first time in 12 years
in BPA's City High history.
So we're really glad and really proud

and we're excited to
see what happens next.
Thank you guys.
- [Malone] Thank you.

- Okay, the last thing
I wanted to talk about
is unfortunately a little bit less light.
I'm sure you can all guess

but I do want to address briefly
the elephant in the room,
which is obviously the budget,
which I know is going to be discussed
probably at length in this meeting.

Now obviously, bear in mind
I'm much less well-informed
on this than any of you are.
So if I say something stupid, forgive me,
but there are going to need to be cuts.
I know that.
And what I am aware of
is that right now the district's policy

is to provide Chromebooks to
every elementary schooler.
I don't know how much Chromebooks cost
or how much of a problem
in terms of the budget that really is,
but they are computers,
I would assume they're somewhat expensive

and with the rise of AI and
more and more reports coming out

about the harm that technology
can play in the classroom,
I would I suppose encourage the board

to think about the role
that technology plays
in classrooms with younger kids.
I do think supporting
or providing a Chromebook,
a free computer to high school students
is a very amazing thing that we do
in terms of equity and accessibility

and I would certainly
encourage that to be continued.
But in the elementary school,
like in the, I suppose, the years

where these kids are
learning what education is
and how to be educated,

the idea that AI or education
could be doing it for them
or they could be trying

to get it to do it for
them is of concern to me
and I think may be an area

where the district is
able to save some money.
I could be completely wrong
but I hope that whatever decision is made

will be able to minimally
affect students and teachers.
Thank you.
- Thank you.
Next up we will have West High.
Waleed and Eddie.
- What's up guys?

I just wanna start it
off with the obvious fact
that these last few meetings,

me and Eddie have been
walking in a little late.
We wanted to just let it be known

that we have Track and
Debate every Tuesday
and we do have reasons to why.
So Eddie you can start it off.

- With that, we're very
happy we were third today.
Hopefully we weren't pushed back
'cause we've got a bit of an update.

First we wanted to
shout out Red Cross Club

for collaborating with
Cane's in Coralville
in order to fundraise for blood donations
and other things that are so hard.
We think it's very notable
and I'm sure they raised a lot of money.
I didn't get an exact dollar amount

but I definitely think it's
worth accounting for here.

Additionally, we know
about the Prom ReRun,
I'm sure you guys do too.
It's districtwide.
It allows people to get prom apparel,
both donations and recipients are able,
like, recipiations, I guess
are able to happen through Prom ReRun

and Iowa City West is
participating in that as well.
So that's definitely pretty cool.
Moreover, just for some club things,
the Muslim Student Association, or MSA,
hosted an Iftar dinner.
I saw some familiar faces there
and we hope you guys enjoyed that as well.
And they are planning
to kind of do a rerun of Epcot Night
called Passport to Flavors,
which includes a ton of cultural clubs
like MSA, SSO, BSU, and et cetera

to, again, bring some cultural
flavors to the community
and kind of help people bond over that.
Moreover, student government,
which included me and Waleed obviously,

had a study session for
the end of Trimester 2

in order to help
everybody study for finals

and it had a big turnout
as well as tutors as well

to help people who were
struggling with their classes
or were worried about their finals.
As for competition clubs,
first starting off with HOSA,
this weekend they had FLC,
I don't know exactly what that stands for

but it's pretty cool and we
got a lot of good placements.
Moreover just like building off of BPA,
what these young men had to say,

we are very proud to
announce that Aydan Thomas
is the statewide president of BPA
as well as Aaron Kang
is the vice president of statewide BPA.

So definitely a lot of
notable accomplishments there.
And moreover, West High did participate
in City High's Math Bowl as well
or math competition as well.

- I want it to be known that
my note card is a Trident cap.
I was writing this in the car.

I did tell you guys last
month that I would try
and bring something that's different

to how it would normally go at
a Board of Directors meeting.
And I think that this year
our senior class especially
is doing something that's very different.

Winston Fan is our president
of our senior class
and I'm the vice president
and we have made a cabinet

for our class to represent
after having people vote.

And we are hosting events
for the senior class.
Obviously they're Senior Assassin,
which is heavily mandated, Mr. Gross

and will be safe for school
regarding the AP test as well.
But we're also hosting Senior Field Day
on our field later in May.
Just to have a fun time.
We've raised upwards of $700 in three days
to be able to fund this
'cause we have movie night,
that is, we have a movie night
that's going to be at the track as well
where we're going to get a big,

it's essentially a
really big trailer night
where we'll have a movie

that the senior class
will vote for to watch
just to bring the community together

and have people just be
able to have a good time.

We also have Seal of Biliteracy
going on around the district

and I personally had like
a specific liking to this

'cause I'm doing the one
in French and Spanish,

but just being in the
room taking it this Monday

had me realize how different
people really were.

I didn't know that until
the Center of Innovation
that we taught that we had an ability

for testing in French,
Chinese or Russian and Chinese
and just so many other languages
that were available to other people.
And it made me just, it made me,
not really, I wouldn't say envious,

but it made me realize just
how awesome people are.
It's a really fun thing to see,

especially being in like
so many extracurriculars

and just coming here hearing
about the other schools.

I think that it's something
that I want it to be known

that there are more things
going on in the district
than people really realize,
especially with BPA at City
or people talking about the budget.
Just people talk and from what I know

that there's a lot of good
things happening here.
(Waleed laughs)

- Thank you.
- Thank you.
- Thank you, guys. Have a good night.
Next up is Community Comment.
Thank you for your interest
in Iowa City Community School District

and for your willingness
to share your comments.

You are reminded to
give your name, address,

and topic on which you
plan to speak about.

During Community Comment
persons may speak to the board
about topics relevant to the district.
Speakers who make comments are reminded

they are responsible
for their own statements
and may be subject to legal action
for those which include hate speech
and that are threatening, harassing,
or defamatory in nature.
It is expected that speakers

will address the board and
each other with civility
and abide by the stated time limits.
All Community Comment directed
at non-agenda items and agenda items

will take place at the
beginning of the meeting

and will be limited to
four minutes per speaker
and five minutes for speakers
who has the assistance of an interpreter.

Speaker's time limit will
be displayed on the iPad

on the ledge in front of
Board Secretary Ms. Colvin.

An alarm will sound once the
speaker's time has expired.
The initial Community Comment period
will be limited to an hour.

Remaining Community Comment,
to the extent necessary,
will take place at the end of the meeting.
The board will not engage
in any discussion during public comment.

The role of the board during
this time is to listen.

Any individual who does not
abide by these stated rules

or otherwise disrupts the
meeting may be asked to leave
and/or referred to law enforcement.

And our first speaker for
tonight will be Angie Rogers.
- Good evening.

My name is Angie Rogers
and I live in Coralville.

I'm here tonight as a
community stakeholder

regarding the financial
crisis facing our district.

I wanna remind the board
of something fundamental.

You are not a rubber stamp
for district administration.
You are an elected governing body
and your job is oversight.
By law and public trust

you are responsible for
overseeing the superintendent
and safeguarding district finances

on behalf of students, staff,
taxpayers, and community.
Director Williams and Malone

were recently quoted in
the "Gazette" saying,

quote, "The board bears
this responsibility.
We are fiduciaries of the district
and we have to do a better job."
End of quote.

And that quote, in
hindsight, end of quote,
the board could have asked more questions.

Acknowledging mistakes after
the fact is not sufficient.

This board must exercise
rigorous oversight in real time.

The core fiduciary duties
of a board member are:

duty of care, meaning be
diligent and informed;
duty of loyalty,

put the community and
district as a whole first;

and the duty to follow
law and district policy.
When the retroactive approval
of the $10 million interfund transfer

was discussed and voted on,
every board member had the duty
to probe administration's request.
Yet the public watched

as only two board members
asked meaningful questions
about how a transfer that size happened
without board approval.

This is unacceptable
governance and oversight.

I also want to address
accountability and fairness.

Board members are elected
to represent the community
and make hard decisions

even when those decisions
are uncomfortable.

When there are close
relationships to the district,
including spouses employed by the district
or close ties to senior leadership,
the board must take extra care

to avoid even the appearance
as conflicted oversight.
Please ask the basic governance questions
family, staff, and taxpayers expect
regarding this former CFO

and the executive cabinet
compensation decisions.

How many candidates applied
for the open CFO position?

If there was more than one,
what were their qualifications?
Who did the CFO report to?
What oversight of this position occurred
over the last three years?
Were there any annual reviews given?
That chain of accountability
must be examined openly and thoroughly.
If you don't know where to start to look,
look at the organizational chart
provided by district leadership,

which can be found in the
March 3rd, 2026 slide deck.

In addition, how are
compensation decisions made

at the executive cabinet
level specifically.
The public deserves clarity

on how executive cabinet
raises are determined,
who approves them,
and what controls or oversight exist

to ensure those decisions
are fair, consistent,
and aligned with budget realities.
Given that the superintendent

is the only employee that
reports to the board,

I believe that the public
deserves transparency
on these matters.
Finally, I urge you to vote no tonight
on reducing classroom staffing.
The proposed cuts total $2.2 million.
It is unacceptable for district leadership

to remain largely
insulated from these cuts

while also proposing
classroom staff reductions.
In addition, Central Administration seems

to continue to add to its
headcount during this crisis.

The board documents for tonight
include a recommendation

for a salary adjustment
for a February 2026 hire
of an enrollment and marketing specialist

with an annual salary over
$53,000 plus benefits.
We are in a financial crisis.

Why is there not a hiring freeze
at Central Administration?
You are elected to lead, not defer.
Our community expects diligence,
independence, and accountability.
Thank you.

- Thank you.
(attendees clap)
Next up, we will have Elisa Meeks.
- Hello, my name is Elisa Meeks
and I'm here to speak to the board tonight
about the budget and class sizes.
I'm a proud West High graduate

who has three children who
attend Iowa City schools.

My own children attended
Kirkwood Elementary.

This is also my 22nd year
as an elementary teacher

in the Iowa City
Community School District.
I love teaching in Iowa City
and have had the privilege
to teach at Horn, Wickham, Lemme,
Online Program, and now Twain.

I was a district mentor during
the 2018-2019 school year

and traveled to Grant Wood,
Hills, Twain, Hoover, and Lucas.

As you can see, I have
been in many places,
seen a lot of classes,

and taught everything from
kindergarten to fourth grade.

Anyone who tells you
class size does not matter
or have serious impacts on learning
has not been in a classroom.

It is one of the highest
contributing factors

to how a student's school
year is going to go.
A teaching colleague of mine
who has 33 students this year
sums up these challenges perfectly.
Less individualized instruction.

It's more difficult to
narrow down skill gaps.
Struggling students get less intervention

or intense intervention
due to large groups.
Advanced students get lost in the mix

and small reading and
math groups are shorted.

The logistical challenges
of trying to meet
with 30+ readers in small groups daily
is nearly impossible to tackle.
Reduced quality and speed of feedback.
Quality feedback is one of

the most research
supported teaching moves,

yet it suffers greatly
with large class sizes.

It takes longer to give
written feedback to each child
and to grade assignments,

lengthening the window
between what they hear
and when they did their work.
This makes the feedback less effective.
Teacher workload.

Large classes drastically
increase teacher workload.

For example, it took hours
outside of contract time

to fully prepare for
parent-teacher conferences.
We don't have enough prep time
to do the work the job requires us to do.
Oftentimes there are not even
30+ conference slots available.
Additionally, behind-the-scenes paperwork,
grading and responding to emails
increases with more students.

Last year I was a single section
of fourth grade at Twain.

I started the year with 29
students and quickly went to 32.

I even had 33 students
in my room at one point.
My classroom is not big enough
to hold 33 students comfortably.
There is no carpet space
and barely enough room for 33 desks.

The environment was
frequently overstimulating
to both students and adults

because of the sheer number of
bodies in such a small space.
This year I have 28
and even that is still a lot of students
for the size of the room.
We all hate the thought

of students sitting in
their desks all day.

Yet, we have no space to
move around for brain breaks
or transition from a circle or carpet area
to desks for movement transitions.
Now you are probably thinking,

"Elisa, we already support
keeping class size low.
That's why we have RAM allocations."

Yes, and yet 32 students in a
classroom is still too high.

The elementary teaching load
demand has never been higher.
Still, this school year,

a fourth grade classroom
has 33 students from day one
and never got a second section.
This is a problem.
I would argue that RAM-3 should not exist.

It doesn't matter what
building you teach in,
30 students, or to be clear,

way less in a classroom
should be the aspiration.

Please know that elementary
teachers in Iowa City

have been asked to do more
and more each and every year.
We cover for each other.
We miss our lunches,

often have no one in the
building for behavior support,

missed preps for meetings
every single week.
And still we show up with so much heart

to try to make things
awesome for our kids.
Budget cuts clearly have to happen.

However, I strongly encourage
you to keep the money
to do so closest to the kids.

- Thank you.
(attendees clap)
Next up, we will have Maka Pilcher-Hayek.

- Hello, my name's Maka
Pilcher-Hayek. I live in Iowa City.

I was looking forward
to not speaking tonight
and then I became aware of an email

that a director in Central
Administration sent

to all building administrators
in elementary and secondary.
The email read in part, "As you know,

the district is navigating a
challenging financial landscape

and is experiencing
heightened public scrutiny.

A small group of colleagues
has drafted a letter of support
for superintendent Matt Degner,
Deputy Superintendent Chase Ramey
and the executive cabinet."
Let's see.
"It calls on us as leaders

to approach this moment
with unity and focus

rather than turning inward
and assigning blame.
We are inviting ICCSD administrators

to add their names in
support of this letter."
And then a letter was attached
for the recipients to add their names to.
I can think of zero scenarios
where an employee would feel comfortable
saying no to this email.
In fact, I'm sure I'm not the only one
who heard from building administrators

that felt intimidated
and coerced to sign it.

The statement also contained
several false statements

and reiterated that turning
inward and assigning blame

is somehow contrary to
the district's interests.
We, of course, know that is not true
and that in fact we cannot move forward
until we find out how we ended up
in the situation we are in.
In the end,

the letter just strikes
me as highly inappropriate
and I encourage the board
to examine whether it was legal to send.

Our building administrators
deserve respect,

way more respect than
this letter gave them.

They, like our teachers and
our staff and our families,
are following the facts.

A lot of this information
is available to the public.
And we're reading it.

Therefore, they, of
course, share our concern
and our frustration

with the Central Administration's
financial mismanagement.

It is affecting all of us
already at a building level.

I think one of the main
messages I hope the board gives
to its buildings, to its administrators,
its teachers and staff,

is that we understand that
they can love this district
and that they serve our students
and they can at the same time
criticize the Central Administration.
Right now if they didn't, it would seem,
it would seem strange.

So I just wanna thank our
building administrators
for having to deal with the situation
that this admin team is putting them in
and apologize and let them know
that the community does see them
and thinks that this was a huge overstep
on the administration's part.
Thank you.

- Thank you.
(attendees clap)
Next up, we will have Laura Westemeyer.

- Hi, good evening. My
name is Laura Westemeyer.
I live in Iowa City.

Our community is questioning
if this board understands
its role of oversight.

Because of your failure,
students are paying the price
and the public trust has been lost.
I'll begin with recent comments

made by former board
member Director Eyestone.
He said board members should remember

there are going to be
loud, pervasive people
in the community
and that you are doing a good job

regardless of what those
loud, pervasive people say.

But I want you to imagine
being one of those voices.

Imagine being Mary who is an
incredible mother, volunteer,
and community member,
plus teaches accounting ethics
at the Tippie College of Business.
Mary has predicted nearly every crisis
this district has faced,
not because she has a telepathic mind,

but because she has a
brilliant one and uses it.
Mary has written you emails, many of them,
and has spoken here numerous times.
She has over and over again warned us
of the next developing crisis.
Before the bond, she urged the district
to move the sixth grade
from elementary to the middle school.

She predicted that we would
overbuild elementary seats

and it would create financial
hardship on our district.
The idea was ignored and scoffed at.

Instead, we added greatly
to out elementary classroom.

And then after all the
new space was built,

the district moved sixth
grade to middle school anyway
and then demolished an elementary school.

Mary warned strongly that
the enrollment projections

used during the bond
campaign were inflated.

Mary's projected numbers
are so much closer
to our current student population.
She expressed great concerns
about hiring an unqualified CFO.
She warned that the 2023 audit was late.
Yet people like Mary are dismissed
as loud, pervasive voices.
And it was just several years ago
when the Iowa Department of Education
investigated our district

and reported a retaliatory
culture by the administration
toward the people who speak out.
So with the reported retaliatory culture,

a board member sitting
right there three months ago

called engaged citizens
loud, pervasive voices.
That should give us all reason to pause
and question whether this leadership
has ever learned from its past.

Director Eyestone also
said when addressing

the board's role regarding
the administration,

"You're not the most
important people here.
Your job is to make their jobs easier."
Respectfully, that is not your role.

Your job is to question
the superintendent,
not to make his job easier.
When a board begins to believe its role
is simply to support administration,
something dangerous happens,
problems grow quietly in the background

and eventually those
problems become crises.

And that is exactly
where we are again today.

This crisis did not
originate in the classroom.

It happened because of
incompetent, dishonest,
and excuse-ridden staff.
Our public is tired

of talking about closing
schools and cutting teachers,
tired of paying interest and penalties

instead of investing that
money in students and teachers.

We do not expect perfection
from our leaders,
but we do expect vigilance and competence.
Strong oversight is not negativity

and it should never be dismissed
as a loud, pervasive voice.

Our community is watching to
see who is willing to speak up
